It addresses the analysis of medical cohort studies where diverse data types are acquired to diagnose or predict clinical outcomes, distinguishing itself from its sibling [Mixed Modality Visualization](5716-mixed-modality-visualization.md) by focusing on multiple subjects rather than heterogeneous data types, while coupling information and scientific visualization to extract patterns affecting subgroups of the whole collection [S1, unofficial].

The evidence supports the claim that the work addresses medical cohort studies with diverse data types (imaging, genetics, blood measurements) to diagnose or predict outcomes, and that it couples information and scientific visualization to extract patterns affecting subgroups. However, the evidence does not support the specific comparative claim that it distinguishes itself from 'Mixed Modality Visualization' by focusing on 'multiple subjects rather than heterogeneous data types.' In fact, the evidence states that the studies involve 'mixed modality data' (heterogeneous data types) acquired from a group of subjects, implying that both multiple subjects and heterogeneous data types are present, rather than being mutually exclusive distinguishing features.
